title: ST changes six hours after CABG
subtitle: A 70-year-old man six hours after three-vessel CABG with new inferior ST elevation, rising vasopressor requirement, and a nurse asking whether this is just the pericardium.
objectives: Build a differential for new ST changes in the first 24 hours after CABG that separates graft-related ischemia from pericardial, metabolic, and native-vessel causes, and state what distinguishes a localized from a diffuse pattern.
Map an ECG territory to the graft that supplies it and use echo for new regional wall motion abnormality as the bedside arbiter.
Explain why a single postoperative troponin is uninterpretable after CABG, and state the Fourth Universal Definition type 5 MI, SCAI, and ARC-2 criteria and why they disagree.
Argue the choice between urgent angiography and surgical re-exploration for suspected early graft failure, and name the factors that decide it.

Recognize and manage RV failure after an RCA-territory infarct in the fresh sternotomy patient, including the tradeoffs between pharmacologic support, IABP, and short-term mechanical circulatory support.

stages.title: Presentation
stages.narrative:
A 70-year-old man with three-vessel coronary disease, preserved LV function, and no prior infarct underwent on-pump CABG this afternoon: left internal thoracic artery to the LAD, a saphenous vein graft to the obtuse marginal, and a saphenous vein graft to the distal RCA. The surgeon's note describes a small, diseased, calcified distal RCA target. Cross-clamp and bypass times were unremarkable. He separated from bypass on a low-dose inotrope and arrived in the CTICU with stable hemodynamics, a right radial arterial line, a PA catheter, and two mediastinal drains with modest output. [REVIEW]

It is now six hours after arrival. Over the last 90 minutes his vasopressor requirement has roughly doubled. Heart rate has drifted from the 80s into the low 100s, paced rhythm off. The nurse has run a 12-lead because the monitor strip looked different: there is new ST elevation in II, III, and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL. The anterior leads are unchanged from the postoperative baseline ECG. Mediastinal drain output has not changed. The nurse asks whether this is just postoperative pericarditis and whether you want to be called again if it does not evolve. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Give your differential for new ST changes six hours after CABG, say what about this ECG argues for or against each item, and list exactly what you will send and what you will look at in the next 20 minutes. Commit before revealing.
questions.modelAnswer:
The differential is best organized by whether the ST changes are localized to one territory or diffuse, because that single distinction does most of the work.

**Localized ST elevation with reciprocal change** points to a vessel or graft problem:

- **Acute graft occlusion**, usually thrombosis at an anastomosis or in a vein graft, occasionally dissection or a technical problem at the distal anastomosis. A small, calcified RCA target is exactly the kind of graft that fails early. [REVIEW]
- **Graft spasm.** Arterial conduits (radial artery most of all, ITA less often) spasm, especially with high catecholamine doses, hypothermia, and alpha-agonist exposure. This patient's RCA graft is a vein, so spasm of the conduit is less likely, but the native RCA itself can spasm at the anastomosis or distal to it. [REVIEW]
- **Air embolism.** Classic for the RCA because its ostium sits anteriorly in a supine patient. Usually declares itself coming off bypass rather than six hours later, so timing argues against it, but it belongs on the list. [REVIEW]
- **Kinking or malposition of a long graft**, particularly a vein graft routed to the distal RCA, which can be compressed or kinked when the chest is closed and the heart fills.
- **Competitive flow** from a native vessel that was not critically stenosed. This reduces graft flow and can predispose to early thrombosis, but on its own it produces ischemia only if the graft was the sole supply, so it is more a mechanism than a diagnosis here.
- **Native disease progression** or plaque rupture proximal to the anastomosis in a territory that was incompletely revascularized.
- **Incomplete revascularization** of a branch that was not grafted (a posterolateral branch, for example) and was poorly protected during the clamp period.

**Diffuse ST elevation without reciprocal change** points to pericardial or global causes: the post-pericardiotomy pattern (concave ST elevation in most leads, PR depression), global ischemia from poor myocardial protection, severe anemia or hypoxemia, hyperkalemia, or cardioplegia washout. These are what the nurse is suggesting. The reciprocal depression in I and aVL is the finding that argues against this. Pericarditis does not produce reciprocal changes outside aVR and V1. [REVIEW]

**What to send and what to look at.** The right order is: look at the patient and the pressures, then the echo, then the labs, because labs will not change the next decision.

- Hemodynamics: MAP, CVP, PA pressures, cardiac output or mixed venous saturation off the PA catheter, lactate. A rising CVP with a falling cardiac output and an inferior ECG change is the RV declaring itself.
- Rhythm: new AV block or junctional rhythm with an inferior pattern is another RCA clue.
- Bedside echo, now, by whoever is there, with a formal study to follow: new regional wall motion abnormality in the inferior and inferoseptal segments, RV size and function, tricuspid regurgitation, and tamponade. New RWMA in the territory of the ECG change is the single most useful bedside finding. If the RV is dilated and the inferior wall is akinetic and both are new compared with the intraoperative TEE, you have mapped the ECG to the graft. [REVIEW]
- Compare with the postoperative baseline ECG and with the intraoperative TEE report. The baseline matters because many post-CABG ECGs show some nonspecific ST change from the start.
- Labs: troponin, with a repeat planned, plus potassium, hemoglobin, and an arterial gas. Troponin is sent to establish a trajectory, not to make the diagnosis. A single postoperative value cannot distinguish the expected injury of cardioplegia, cannulation, and manipulation from a new infarct. What matters is a value that is still rising or rising again at a time when the surgical troponin curve should be flat or falling, interpreted alongside the ECG and echo. [REVIEW]
- Drain output and chest radiograph for mediastinal widening if tamponade is in play.
- Call the surgeon early, before the labs are back, with the ECG, the hemodynamic trend, and the echo. The surgeon knows how that RCA anastomosis looked and whether flow was measured on the graft. That information shapes everything that follows.

The answer to the nurse: no, this is not pericarditis, and please do not wait for it to evolve.

questions.prompt: A single postoperative troponin comes back substantially elevated. Which of the following is the correct interpretation: it confirms a perioperative MI, it rules out a perioperative MI if it falls below a published threshold, or it is uninterpretable on its own? Name the published thresholds for post-CABG MI and explain why they disagree.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Best answer: A single value is uninterpretable on its own.** Every CABG causes myocardial injury. Cardioplegic arrest, cannulation, manipulation, and reperfusion all release troponin, and the magnitude depends on the assay, the operation, the clamp time, and the protection strategy. The biomarker only acquires meaning when it is placed on a time course and combined with another sign of ischemia: new ECG changes, new RWMA on imaging, or angiographic graft occlusion.

The published definitions, which the fellow should know as definitions and not as facts about the patient:

- **Fourth Universal Definition of MI (Thygesen 2018), type 5 (CABG-related) MI:** troponin above 10 times the 99th percentile upper reference limit within 48 hours of surgery in a patient with a normal baseline, plus at least one of new pathological Q waves or new LBBB, angiographically documented new graft or native coronary occlusion, or imaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium in a pattern consistent with ischemia. Isolated biomarker elevation above the threshold without the second criterion is classified as myocardial injury, not infarction. [VERIFY]
- **SCAI definition (Moussa 2013) of clinically relevant MI after CABG:** CK-MB at or above 10 times the upper limit of normal, or troponin at or above 70 times, when the baseline is normal, without requiring a second criterion, with lower thresholds (CK-MB 5 times, troponin 35 times) when accompanied by new Q waves or new LBBB. [VERIFY]
- **ARC-2 (Garcia-Garcia 2018):** for CABG, troponin at or above 35 times the upper reference limit, or CK-MB at or above 10 times, with at least one ancillary criterion (new Q waves or LBBW on ECG, imaging evidence, or angiographic loss of graft or native vessel patency). [VERIFY]

Why they disagree: the Universal Definition is a pathophysiologic definition built around the diagnosis of infarction in the individual patient. SCAI and ARC-2 were built to count prognostically meaningful events in trials, and they set the biomarker bar where the association with mortality became convincing. The newest data push the bar higher still. In the VISION Cardiac Surgery cohort (Devereaux and colleagues, NEJM 2022), the high-sensitivity troponin I level associated with increased 30-day mortality after CABG or AVR was roughly 218 times the upper reference limit on the first postoperative day, far above the Universal Definition's 10 times threshold, which was crossed by most patients with an uneventful course. [VERIFY]

The ESC joint working group position paper (Thielmann 2017) says, in effect, that no biomarker threshold alone defines perioperative MI after CABG and that the diagnosis must integrate ECG, echo, hemodynamics, and where indicated angiography. That is the practical stance to take at the bedside. [VERIFY]

Why the alternatives fall short:

- **It confirms a perioperative MI.** Only if the value exceeds the definitional threshold and there is a second criterion. In this patient there is an ECG criterion, and an echo criterion may follow, so the diagnosis may well be made. But the troponin did not make it.
- **It rules out MI if below a threshold.** The thresholds were chosen for prognosis in populations, not for sensitivity in individuals, and a value drawn six hours after an occlusion may not yet have peaked. A reassuring single value in a patient with new regional ST elevation and new RWMA should not reassure anyone.

The assay-specific 99th percentile and whatever troponin schedule the unit uses after CABG are institutional. [NMH protocol, insert]

stages.title: New data
stages.narrative:
The bedside echo, compared with the intraoperative TEE, shows new hypokinesis of the basal and mid inferior wall and inferoseptum. The RV is mildly dilated and sluggish, with reduced free wall motion that was not present at the end of the case. There is a small, non-circumferential posterior collection without chamber compression. Anterior and lateral walls move as they did intraoperatively. [REVIEW]

Hemodynamics are worse. The vasopressor has been increased again, the CVP has climbed, the PA pressures have not, the cardiac index has fallen, and mixed venous saturation is lower than at admission. Lactate has risen modestly. The rhythm is now intermittently junctional. Potassium, hemoglobin, and gas are unremarkable. Troponin is elevated with no earlier postoperative value to compare. [REVIEW]

The surgeon is on the phone. She notes that the distal RCA target was poor, that graft flow on the transit-time probe was lower than the other grafts but accepted, and that she is in the middle of another case for the next hour. The cath lab says they could have a table in about 40 minutes. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Lay out the options now (vasodilator for suspected spasm, urgent angiography, return to the OR, IABP, more support and wait) and commit to a sequence. Say what should happen in parallel and what determines angiography versus re-exploration.
questions.modelAnswer:
The echo has converted a suspicion into a diagnosis: inferior and RV ischemia in the territory of the RCA graft, with hemodynamic consequence. The question is no longer whether but how to restore flow.

**Options and how they fit:**

- **Nitroglycerin, and a calcium channel blocker if an arterial conduit is involved.** For suspected spasm, this is cheap and fast. Intravenous nitroglycerin is reasonable as a first move while the rest is being arranged, accepting that it will cost preload in an RV that already needs it and will need to be balanced with the vasopressor. The argument for a calcium channel blocker is strongest for radial artery conduits. This graft is a vein and the ECG has persisted for over an hour with a wall motion abnormality, which makes fixed obstruction more likely than spasm. A trial of nitroglycerin that does not improve the ST segments within minutes should not delay anything else. [REVIEW]
- **Urgent coronary angiography.** This is the diagnostic step that tells you what the problem is and, in many cases, fixes it. The ESC working group position paper and the subsequent literature favor angiography as the first step in the hemodynamically stable or stabilizable patient with suspected early graft failure, because about a third of such patients have no graft problem on angiography and would have gone back to the OR for nothing, and because PCI can treat many of the lesions found. In the Biancari meta-analysis of control angiography for perioperative ischemia, about 62 percent had acute graft failure, and among those revascularized roughly half had PCI and half had reoperation, with no significant difference in early mortality between the two. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]
- **Return to the OR.** Appropriate when the patient is too unstable to survive transport and a diagnostic study, when tamponade or bleeding is the likely cause, when the surgeon has a specific technical concern she wants to look at directly, or when the cath lab is not available in a useful time frame. Re-exploration without angiography treats the chest as the diagnosis, and a third of the time it is not. [REVIEW]
- **IABP.** Augments diastolic coronary perfusion pressure and reduces LV afterload. For RV ischemia the benefit is indirect: it raises aortic diastolic pressure and therefore RCA perfusion pressure, and it supports whatever LV dysfunction accompanies the inferior infarct. It is reasonable to place in the cath lab at the time of angiography, or in the unit if transport is the barrier. It does not treat RV preload or afterload problems directly. [REVIEW]
- **More support and wait.** The option that loses. A thrombosed vein graft to an RV-supplying RCA does not get better with norepinephrine, and the RV is the chamber that tolerates time poorly.

**The committed sequence:** start nitroglycerin if the pressure allows, keep the RV filled but not overfilled, treat the junctional rhythm with pacing through the epicardial wires to restore AV synchrony, and take the patient to the cath lab as soon as the table is open, with the surgeon aware and the OR on standby. The surgeon's description of the graft (a poor target, low transit-time flow) makes a technical or thrombotic problem at that anastomosis the leading diagnosis and makes it exactly the kind of lesion the interventionalist can look at and often treat. [REVIEW]

**In parallel:** a second large-bore access, blood available, heparin decision made with the surgeon before the sheath goes in, a plan for who manages the airway and the pressors during transport, and the ECMO team aware in case the patient deteriorates on the table.

**What determines angiography versus re-exploration:**

1. **Which graft.** An ITA to the LAD that has failed is a surgical problem more often than not, because the conduit is precious and the fix is usually a technical revision. A vein graft to a small RCA is often a PCI problem or, if the target is as poor as described, a problem that may be better left to the native vessel.
2. **How unstable.** A patient who cannot be moved safely does not get angiography. The threshold for that is judgment, and the threshold is lower when the surgeon is already scrubbed in the next room.
3. **What else is in the differential.** If tamponade, bleeding, or a mechanical problem is plausible, the OR answers more questions than the cath lab.
4. **Availability.** Forty minutes to a cath lab table versus a surgeon who is an hour away changes the calculus. These are local facts. [NMH protocol, insert]

**How to involve the surgeon:** early, with the data (ECG, echo findings in territory terms, hemodynamic trajectory), with a proposed plan rather than a question, and with the recognition that the surgeon's description of the anastomosis is a piece of data you cannot get anywhere else. The conversation about angiography first is easier when it is framed as the thing that tells her whether she needs to reopen.

stages.title: Decision point
stages.narrative: In the cath lab, with an IABP placed on arrival, angiography shows a patent LITA to the LAD with brisk flow and a patent vein graft to the obtuse marginal. The vein graft to the distal RCA is occluded at its distal anastomosis with thrombus. The native RCA has a long, calcified, diffusely diseased mid and distal segment with a severe stenosis proximal to the anastomosis, and a small, poorly opacified posterior descending artery. The interventionalist is on the phone with the surgeon. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: PCI of the graft, PCI of the native RCA, or surgical revision: which do you support and why? Then set out the antiplatelet and anticoagulation plan for a patient whose sternotomy is nine hours old.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Best answer: PCI of the native RCA, if the interventionalist judges the lesion treatable, with surgical revision held in reserve.** The reasoning is about which target is most likely to stay open and what each option costs this particular patient.

- **PCI of the native RCA.** The graft failed, most likely, because it was sewn to a poor target with low flow. Recanalizing and stenting the native proximal stenosis restores flow through the vessel's own distribution, including branches the graft never served, and avoids a fresh vein graft anastomosis that just thrombosed. The cost is a long, calcified lesion that may need atherectomy, a small distal bed that limits the benefit, and a stent that commits the patient to dual antiplatelet therapy in a fresh chest. If the lesion is treatable, most interventionalists and surgeons would favor this. The ESC working group paper and the 2021 ACC/AHA/SCAI revascularization guideline both discuss PCI as an option for early graft failure, with the choice between PCI and reoperation made jointly by the heart team on anatomy and stability. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]
- **PCI of the graft.** Crossing and stenting a freshly thrombosed distal vein graft anastomosis is technically possible but the substrate is bad: fresh suture line, thrombus, small distal vessel, and a high risk of distal embolization and re-thrombosis. Most interventionalists would choose the native vessel when it is accessible.
- **Surgical revision.** Re-exploration and redo of the distal anastomosis, or a new graft to a different RCA branch, is the right answer when the native vessel cannot be treated percutaneously, when the problem is clearly technical (a kinked graft, a stenotic anastomosis), or when the patient is too unstable to tolerate a long interventional procedure. The cost is a second bypass run or an off-pump redo on a stunned RV in a patient nine hours out, with the bleeding and myocardial protection problems that implies. Surgical mortality for early re-revascularization is not trivial in the series that report it. [REVIEW]

**Antithrombotic plan in the fresh chest.** This is a negotiation among three people with different fears: the interventionalist (stent thrombosis), the surgeon (mediastinal bleeding and tamponade), and the intensivist (both).

- **Aspirin** is already due. Every post-CABG patient should receive aspirin within the first hours after surgery, and there is no reason to withhold it here. [REVIEW]
- **P2Y12 inhibitor.** If a stent is placed, a P2Y12 inhibitor is required. The choice of agent is a judgment call: clopidogrel has the slowest onset and the least bleeding, ticagrelor is more potent and reversible in principle but bleeds more, prasugrel is generally avoided after CABG. In a nine-hour-old chest with drains in place, many centers load clopidogrel and defer the more potent agents until the drains are out and the bleeding risk has declined. The guideline support for dual antiplatelet therapy after CABG exists independent of stenting, so the stent only sharpens the decision. The agent and timing are a heart team decision and institutional. [NMH protocol, insert] [REVIEW]
- **Procedural heparin** during PCI is unavoidable. Reversal with protamine after the procedure is a judgment call that trades stent thrombosis against bleeding, and many centers let it wear off rather than reverse it. [REVIEW]
- **Therapeutic anticoagulation** afterward is not indicated for the stent and should not be started for the graft. The IABP needs only what the institution uses for balloon pumps. [NMH protocol, insert]
- **Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors** are the thing to argue against. They are occasionally used for large thrombus burden in the cath lab, and in a patient with mediastinal drains they turn a manageable bleeding risk into a tamponade risk. If the interventionalist proposes one, the conversation about drain output and the surgeon's threshold for reopening should happen before it is given. [REVIEW]

After the procedure, mediastinal drain output is watched hourly, and the threshold for return to the OR for bleeding is lower than it would otherwise be, because this patient now has three antithrombotic exposures and a stunned RV that will not tolerate tamponade.

stages.title: Complication
stages.narrative: The native RCA is successfully stented and TIMI 3 flow is restored to the posterior descending artery. The ST segments improve but do not normalize. Back in the CTICU two hours later, the picture is RV failure: CVP is high and climbing, PA pressures are low to normal, cardiac index is poor despite the IABP and an escalating inotrope, the liver is congested on ultrasound, urine output has stopped, and lactate is rising. Echo shows a dilated, severely hypokinetic RV with a flattened septum, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and an underfilled LV with preserved contraction. The posterior collection is unchanged and there is no chamber compression. Drain output is modest and stable. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Manage this RV failure. Say what you will do with volume, rhythm, afterload, inotropes, and the IABP, and then make the case for which form of mechanical circulatory support you would choose if that fails, given that the sternotomy is twelve hours old.
questions.modelAnswer:
The pathophysiology is an ischemic, reperfused, and stunned RV that cannot deliver preload to a normal LV. The management is to optimize the RV on each axis in turn, recognizing that most of the levers have a cost.

- **Volume.** The reflex is to give it. The echo says the RV is already dilated and the septum is flattened, which means more volume will push the septum further into the LV, worsen LV filling, and raise RV wall stress. This patient needs no more preload and may benefit from careful removal. The right test is to give a small bolus and look at the septum and the cardiac index, not to chase the CVP. [REVIEW]
- **Rhythm.** AV synchrony and rate matter more for a failing RV than for almost any other patient. A-V pacing through the epicardial wires at a rate that optimizes output, with atrial contribution preserved, is cheap and often underused. [REVIEW]
- **RV afterload.** The PA pressures are not high, so this is not primarily an afterload problem, but every contributor should be removed: hypoxemia, hypercapnia, acidosis, high airway pressures, and excessive PEEP. Inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (nitric oxide or prostacyclin) lower RV afterload without systemic hypotension and are reasonable even when the PVR is not strikingly elevated, because the RV's tolerance of afterload is lowest when it is ischemic. [REVIEW]
- **Coronary perfusion pressure.** The RV is perfused in systole and diastole, and a stunned RV with a fresh stent in its feeding artery is exquisitely sensitive to systemic hypotension. Maintaining MAP with a vasopressor is RV therapy, not a concession. The IABP contributes here by raising diastolic aortic pressure. [REVIEW]
- **Inotropes.** Dobutamine or milrinone, either with a vasopressor to protect MAP. Milrinone lowers PVR and is the usual choice for RV failure, but it causes systemic hypotension and has a long half-life. Epinephrine offers inotropy with pressor effect but at the cost of tachycardia and lactate. Low-dose combinations are common. There is no trial to point to. [REVIEW]
- **The IABP** stays. It is doing something useful for coronary perfusion pressure, even if it is not RV support in the mechanical sense.

**If that fails: which MCS.** The options in a twelve-hour-old sternotomy:

- **Percutaneous RV assist device (RA to PA, with or without an oxygenator).** A dual-lumen cannula placed through the internal jugular vein that drains the RA and ejects into the PA provides direct RV bypass without a second sternotomy, can be placed in the cath lab or at the bedside with TEE or fluoroscopy, and can have an oxygenator added if the lungs fail. It unloads the RV directly, which VA ECMO does only partially. This is the best fit for isolated RV failure with a working LV and working lungs. The limitations are flow ceiling, the need for a competent LV, and the need for fluoroscopy at many centers. [REVIEW]
- **Peripheral VA ECMO.** The fastest to deploy and the most familiar. It supports both ventricles and the lungs. The cost is LV afterload, which in this patient with a normal LV is tolerable, and the fact that it bypasses rather than unloads the RV: a dilated RV may stay dilated on VA ECMO. It is the right choice if the LV is also failing, if there is hypoxemia, or if deterioration is too fast for anything more selective. [REVIEW]
- **Surgically placed RVAD through the sternotomy.** The chest is already open in the sense that reopening is a short operation, and a central RA-to-PA cannulation with a centrifugal pump gives high flow and direct unloading. The cost is an open chest, bleeding, infection, and a sternotomy that must eventually be closed. It is the choice when the surgeon is already going back in for another reason, or when percutaneous access fails. [REVIEW]
- **Microaxial RV pump** (a percutaneous axial device placed through the femoral vein across the tricuspid and pulmonic valves) is an alternative at centers with experience, with the same indication as the percutaneous RA-to-PA device and different limitations on position and durability. [REVIEW]

**The committed choice:** a percutaneous RA-to-PA RVAD, placed in the cath lab under fluoroscopy, before the lactate and the liver tell you the window has closed. The argument is that the problem is isolated RV failure with a functioning LV and lungs, the device unloads the chamber that is failing, and it avoids reopening the chest. VA ECMO is the fallback if the patient arrests or the LV fails. The timing is the hard part: the mortality of MCS placed after multiorgan failure has set in is the reason to go early. [REVIEW]

Two things to say to the surgeon before any of this: the plan for anticoagulation on the device in a patient with drains, and the plan for what happens to the sternum if the device fails and the chest has to be reopened. [NMH protocol, insert]

teachingPoints:
- New ST changes after CABG are graft-related until proven otherwise. The single most useful discriminator at the bedside is localized versus diffuse: localized elevation with reciprocal change is a vessel or graft, diffuse elevation without reciprocal change is the pericardium or a global insult.
- Map the ECG territory to the graft that serves it, then confirm with echo for new regional wall motion abnormality compared with the intraoperative TEE. The echo converts suspicion into diagnosis and defines the hemodynamic consequence.
- A single postoperative troponin is uninterpretable after CABG. Trajectory plus a second criterion (ECG, imaging, angiography) makes the diagnosis. The Universal Definition, SCAI, and ARC-2 thresholds differ because they were built for different purposes, and recent cohort data place the prognostic threshold far higher than any of them. [VERIFY]
- Angiography first is the default for suspected early graft failure in a patient who can be moved. About a third have no graft problem, and PCI treats many of those who do. Re-exploration first is for the patient who cannot be moved, has a likely surgical cause, or has a surgeon with a specific technical concern. [REVIEW]
- Native-vessel PCI is often preferred over graft PCI when the graft failed because of a poor target. The antithrombotic plan after stenting a nine-hour-old chest is a negotiation, and glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors are the thing to argue against. [REVIEW]
- RV failure after an RCA-territory infarct is managed by removing preload rather than adding it when the septum is flattened, by restoring AV synchrony, by protecting coronary perfusion pressure, and by lowering RV afterload. When that fails, a percutaneous RA-to-PA RVAD unloads the failing chamber without reopening the chest. Go early. [REVIEW]
- Call the surgeon before the labs are back, with territory-mapped findings and a proposed plan. The surgeon's description of the anastomosis is data you cannot get anywhere else.
pitfalls:
- Accepting pericarditis as the explanation for regional ST elevation with reciprocal change. Pericarditis is diffuse.
- Waiting for troponin to decide whether this is an infarct. The next decision does not depend on it.
- Re-exploring without angiography when the patient could have been moved. A third of the time there is nothing to fix surgically, and the second bypass run is not free.
- Treating suspected spasm with nitroglycerin and then waiting to see if it works while the RV declines. A trial of vasodilator should not delay definitive imaging.
- Filling a dilated RV with a flattened septum because the CVP is being read as a preload target.
- Letting the MAP drift in a patient with a stunned RV and a fresh stent in its feeding artery. RV coronary perfusion pressure is the first thing to protect.
- Agreeing to a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor in a patient with mediastinal drains without a conversation about the surgeon's threshold for reopening.
- Waiting until the lactate and liver function have declared multiorgan failure before placing mechanical support.
controversies:
**What defines a perioperative MI after CABG.** The Fourth Universal Definition requires troponin above 10 times the upper reference limit plus a second criterion. SCAI and ARC-2 use higher biomarker thresholds chosen for trial endpoints. The VISION Cardiac Surgery cohort found that the threshold associated with mortality after CABG was more than an order of magnitude higher than the Universal Definition's. The consequence is that the same patient can have a type 5 MI by one definition and uncomplicated surgery by another, and the literature on outcomes after perioperative MI is only as comparable as the definitions it used. The ESC working group's position that no biomarker threshold alone makes the diagnosis is the practical compromise. [VERIFY] [REVIEW]

**Angiography versus re-exploration.** No randomized trial exists and none will. The angiography-first argument rests on diagnostic yield (a third of patients have no graft problem) and on PCI as a less morbid fix. The re-exploration-first argument rests on speed in the unstable patient, on the surgeon's ability to see and fix technical problems that angiography cannot characterize, and on avoiding the radiation and contrast of a study that may lead back to the OR anyway. Center infrastructure (a hybrid OR, a cath lab in the same building, a surgeon who is available) determines practice more than evidence does. [NMH protocol, insert]

**Routine postoperative troponin after CABG.** Some centers measure troponin on a schedule after every CABG and use the trajectory to screen for silent graft failure. Others measure it only when the ECG or echo raises concern, on the grounds that the expected rise is wide, the prognostic threshold is uncertain, and a routine value changes management rarely. The VISION data make a case for routine measurement as a prognostic tool, not as a diagnostic one. [REVIEW]

**Graft spasm prophylaxis.** Calcium channel blockers after radial artery grafting were standard for years on the basis of early series and conduit physiology. Later randomized data and registry analyses did not consistently show benefit, and the 2021 ACC/AHA/SCAI revascularization guideline addresses radial artery conduits without mandating a specific antispasm regimen. Many surgeons still use a calcium channel blocker for weeks to months after radial grafting. Whether intravenous nitroglycerin should be routine for the first postoperative night in arterial-conduit patients is a center preference. [VERIFY] [NMH protocol, insert]

**RV mechanical support selection.** Percutaneous RA-to-PA devices, microaxial RV pumps, surgical RVADs, and VA ECMO all have advocates. There is no comparative trial, and selection depends on whether the LV and lungs are working, whether the chest is open or openable, and what the center can deploy at 2 a.m. [REVIEW]
discussWithAttending: The surgeon on the phone says she would rather reopen than send the patient to the cath lab, because she wants to see the anastomosis. Make the case for angiography first, then argue her side.
If this had been the LITA to the LAD that failed rather than a vein graft to a small RCA, how would the choice between PCI and surgical revision change, and why?
Where is your threshold for placing mechanical RV support in a patient twelve hours after sternotomy, and what single variable would move it earlier?

The interventionalist proposes a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa infusion for thrombus burden in a patient with mediastinal drains. What do you need to know from the surgeon before saying yes, and what would make you say no?
